title: The wounds (La Verna, 1224)
hookLine: near the end of his life, Francis receives the marks of the wounds of Christ

cards: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Saint Paul wrote that to the Galatians, near the end of his letter.
In another letter he lists beatings and a stoning, and some readers take the marks to be those scars, earned on the road.
Now carry that sentence up a wooded mountain in Tuscany called La Verna, where Francis has gone with a few brothers to fast and pray, away from everyone. He is ill and worn out.
What happens on that mountain gives Paul's word a new life: stigmata.

teach.h: A SERAPH, AND A MAN ON A CROSS.
teach.b: Thomas of Celano and Saint Bonaventure both tell it. While Francis prays, he sees a figure like a seraph, the angel of Isaiah's vision, with six wings, and between the wings a man fixed to a cross.
Francis is torn between joy at the beauty of it and grief at the suffering, and he doesn't understand what he has seen.

teach.h: NAILS, AND A WOUND IN THE SIDE.
teach.b: When the vision fades, the accounts say, the signs of nails appear in his hands and feet, and a wound opens in his side. Not paint, not a vision any more, but wounds he has to wrap.
He didn't show them off. Celano says he hid them with great care, covering his hands, wearing something on his feet, and only a few close brothers knew while he lived.
The marks were something given, and he guarded them like a secret between friends.

The Church reads the stigmata not as a magic trick but as love made visible: Francis had spent years trying to follow Christ in poverty and humility, and his body, the tradition says, came to carry the shape of that love.

teach.h: I BEAR THE MARKS OF THE LORD JESUS.
teach.b: Paul's word for the marks became the Church's word for this. Franciscans keep a feast of the stigmata of Saint Francis, and La Verna is still a place of prayer.
Some readers take the accounts as a miracle exactly as told, and some ask what the brothers saw and how they described it. Either way, it's the story of a man marked by love.

how: Franciscans keep a feast of the Stigmata of Saint Francis, and Franciscan friars care for the sanctuary at La Verna, where pilgrims still come to pray at the place of the vision.

games.q: you're Francis. you come down from the mountain with wounds in your hands and feet. what do you do?
o: hide them, and tell only a few close brothers.
leave the order and live alone.
games.why: he covered them and guarded them like a secret. the marks were not a trophy.

practice: Name one person to yourself who is sick, grieving, or hurting in a way you can see or one they've only told you about.
Don't try to fix anything: if you pray, say their name to God and stay with it, and if you don't, keep them in your attention gently, the way you'd sit beside a hospital bed.

wordCard.voice: Stigmata. Paul's word for the marks of Jesus that he bore, and the Church's word for the wounds of Christ that Francis received on La Verna. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: marks, brands. Paul uses it in Galatians 6:17 for the marks of Jesus on his body.
